newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FEATURE - Telecom gets pre-election nerves.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Telecom gets pre-election nerves.

text.p: Two weeks before a general election, New Zealand's biggest company Telecom Corp is nervously awaiting an outcome that could wind back one of the most deregulated telecommunications markets in the world.

On current polling, the three main opposition parties will have the numbers to end six years of conservative National Party government when the country goes to the polls on October 12 -- and all three have expressed varying reservations about the existing "light-handed" telecoms regulations.

A symptom of Telecom's nervousness was chairman Peter Shirtcliffe's speech last week to an Australian business forum when he warned Australians that their $20 billion investment in New Zealand could be under threat if populist politicians -- shorthand for opposition parties New Zealand First and the Alliance -- win power proposing "short-sighted controls on economic activity".
He said the left-wing Alliance and economic nationalist New Zealand First wanted to see "the heavy hand of State controlling the affairs of business".

Both parties want to place limits of 24.9 percent on certain foreign shareholdings, although their criteria differ. Neither would force the sale of existing shareholdings, but both have pledged to reverse the government's August sale of Forestry Corporation for $1.6 billion to a consortium led by Fletcher Forest.
OPPOSITION HAS RESERVATIONS ABOUT TELECOM REGIME

More significantly for Telecom, the Alliance, and to a lesser extent New Zealand First and the main opposition Labour Party, have misgivings about the effectiveness of the existing light-handed telecommunications regime.
This uses the Commerce Act and anti-trust Commerce Commission to control monopolistic practice. There are no industry-specific watchdogs.
Communications Minister Maurice Williamson is fond of waving a blank piece of paper in front of industry groups to demonstrate the country's lack of entry barriers to the telecommunications industry.
But the Alliance has used former state-owned Telecom's level of profits and market dominance as a campaign theme, saying it exploits a lack of competition.

Alliance leader Jim Anderton has a personal stake in bringing Telecom to heel. He resigned from Labour in 1989 over its sale of Telecom to a consortium led by U.S companies Ameritech Corp and Bell Atlantic, each of which owns a quarter of the company.
Anderton has promised to cut Telecom's residential line charges by 30 percent and remove its control of the telephone numbering system if his party wins office.
His most recent spat with Shirtcliffe took the rhetoric between the two to new heights, with Anderton saying Shirtcliffe was "right to be afraid -- very, very afraid" of the Alliance.
Anderton has allies for some of his complaints.

New entrants to the market Clear Communications, BellSouth NZ and Australia's Telstra, and even some in government, are not convinced a hands-off approach has delivered true competition over the whole range of services.

A joint Treasury-Commerce Ministry paper on the rules governing vertically-integrated monopolies, released in 1995 (prompted by a long running dispute about access for Clear to Telecom's network) was equivocal about the need for change, while pointing to Telecom's high returns.
After 10 months consideration of the options raised by the report -- including industry-specific rules and arbitration mechanisms -- Williamson chose to stay with the status quo.
But Clear, which says there is still no effective competition for residential users, expressed its disappointment with the government's hands-off approach to the report.
Clear wants industry-specific rules developed through the Telecommunications Act.
"There can be no true competition when one incumbent controls access, the price of access, and the contractual terms of access," Clear corporate communications manager Janiene Bayliss told Reuters.
"We are looking for intervention as opposed to regulation."
TELECOME FAVOURS STATUS QUO
Not surprisingly, Telecom favours the status quo and points to Clear's profitability and a 95 percent penetration of telephones into residential houses as proof of consumer satisfaction.

Williamson has promised action on a couple of the major bones of contention -- telephone number portability and the cost of interconnection to Telecom's system -- if negotiations are not carried out in good faith.

He would also consider legislation barring the application of the so-called Baumol-Willig rule, approved by the Privy Council in a court case between Clear and Telecom, that allows monopolies to recover lost opportunity costs when a competitor enters the market.
Given Williamson's free-market leanings, industry players see little likelihood of his threats being carried out.

But Clear's Bayliss sees change as inevitable afer the election. "I don't think things will ever be the way they were in the past. There will be change regardless of the government. Parliament in general is aware the consumer is not happy."
She is not concerned about the changes, however, and says even the Alliance's position is often misunderstood.
"They are quoted more on intervention but they are...saying if competition is not delivering benefits across the market they will regulate in the interests of getting competition."

The other major opposition party, Labour, wants to establish a universal service obligation requiring telecommunications providers to ensure reasonable access for all households. But in general it, too, favours effective competition over regulation.

Together Labour, the Alliance and New Zealand First are drawing 50 percent support in recent polls against 38.5 percent for the ruling National Party. National's likely coalition partners are struggling to attract enough support to win seats.
New Zealand First has just under 20 percent support in recent polls while the Alliance has 14 percent, ensuring them considerable influence in any centre-left government.
